lesson.title: Does It Add Up? Testing a Distribution for Validity
lesson.summary: A probability distribution is only valid if every probability is between 0 and 1 and the probabilities of all possible values sum to exactly 1, guaranteeing that something in the list is certain to happen.
lesson.body:
A probability distribution is not automatically legitimate just because someone wrote numbers next to a list of values. Before you trust a distribution enough to calculate anything from it, you need to check that it satisfies two conditions. First, every individual probability P(x) must satisfy 0 is less than or equal to P(x), and P(x) is less than or equal to 1, since a probability, by definition, can never be negative and can never exceed 1. Second, the probabilities of all the possible values must sum to exactly 1, because the list of values is meant to cover every possible outcome, and something has to happen.

Check these two conditions against the pets distribution from the previous chapter: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.4, 0.3, and 0.1. Every one of those four numbers is between 0 and 1, so the first condition holds. Adding them up, 0.2 + 0.4 + 0.3 + 0.1 = 1.0 exactly, so the second condition holds too. This confirms the pets distribution used in earlier examples is genuinely valid.

Now look at what can go wrong. Suppose someone proposed the following distribution for the same variable: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.3, 0.4, 0.3, and 0.2. Every individual number is between 0 and 1, so the first condition looks fine at a glance. But adding them up gives 0.3 + 0.4 + 0.3 + 0.2 = 1.2, which is not equal to 1. This fails the second condition, so it cannot be a valid probability distribution, no matter how reasonable each individual number looked in isolation. Errors like this happen in practice when someone estimates each probability a little too generously and the small excesses add up.

Here is a second kind of failure. Suppose instead the proposed probabilities were negative 0.1, 0.5, 0.4, and 0.2 for x = 0, 1, 2, 3. Adding these up gives negative 0.1 + 0.5 + 0.4 + 0.2 = 1.0, so the second condition, summing to 1, is satisfied. But the very first entry, negative 0.1, is less than 0, which is impossible for a probability. This fails the first condition even though the total came out correctly. The lesson here is important: satisfying only one of the two conditions is not enough, both must hold at the same time for a distribution to be valid.

These checks are not just a formality. Every calculation covered later in this unit, expected value, variance, standard deviation, sums and differences of random variables, assumes you are starting from a valid distribution. If the probabilities do not sum to 1, it usually means an outcome was left out of the list, an outcome was accidentally counted twice, or an arithmetic mistake was made somewhere upstream, and any calculation built on top of that broken foundation would be wrong. Get in the habit of adding up the probabilities and scanning for negative or oversized values before doing anything else with a distribution.
